meta.method_note: Six isolated agent contexts · parallel review · cross-examination · moderated synthesis
meta.finding_key_format: Every finding has a unique finding_key of the form '<reviewer>:<finding_id>', e.g. 'adversarial-qa:F2'. Cross-references elsewhere in this file use finding_key.
meta.finding_id_normalization: Reviewers labeled findings differently ('Finding 1', '1.', '#1', 'F1'). All are normalized to F1-F5; the original label is kept in original_label. Adversarial QA's new Round 2 finding (from its connection X3) has no ID in the source and is assigned F6 here.

reviewers.lens: Core loop, progression, pacing, difficulty, resource/economy math
Story logic, character motivation, tone, theme, dialogue intent
What a real player feels in the first hour, the first week, and the moment they decide whether to come back
Technical feasibility against 2026 constraints: 7-week schedule, one human Director plus AI dev crew, browser three.js/WebGPU client
Contradictions, edge cases, exploits, unplanned fail states
Feature creep, core vs. decoration, market positioning, audience clarity, one game or several

findings.title: “The day's real decision” has no numbers, no visible stakes, and a failure case nobody handles
findings.description: The document makes night-shift allocation the main strategic choice (“Choosing what gets the frontier desks is the day's real decision”) but never models it. There is no number of frontier desks and nothing says what sets it. Nothing says what you give up: the night crew is free ($0 in fees) and no passage says what frontier desks do better (quality, speed, task types), so with no visible difference the obvious play is to send everything to the free crew. The resource actually spent is usage caps (about 2.5M tokens per task, about 3 tasks per session), which the game never shows, so the player allocates without seeing what they spend. And a “!” can only come from ask_player while the door locks at closing time, so a frontier desk that hits a question at 1 a.m. has nowhere to send it; whether it stalls, skips ahead, or guesses decides whether the “real decision” is a decision or a gamble.
findings.passage_referenced: §2 A day is one round, step 4 (“Choosing what gets the frontier desks is the day's real decision”) and step 5 (“the door locks until morning”); §3 twin rule (ask_player); §4 Token budget and the usage-caps paragraph
findings.omission_noted: No desk count, no frontier-vs-local quality difference, no visible usage-cap resource, no rule for a blocked night worker
findings.fix_direction: Make capacity an in-world resource with a count (N desks lit, with a gauge mapping to the real cap window). Show frontier vs. local output difference as blueprints at breakfast. Define what a blocked night worker does, e.g. “parks with a note on the board.”
findings.round2_change_note: Kept MAJOR, strengthened: the opening scene shows a worker “stuck at 3 a.m.” as atmosphere, not a rule (QA F3); Feasibility F1 confirms the system isn't scheduled. Recommends either cutting night-shift allocation from v1 or modeling it with numbers.

findings.title: Chapter wins are a 7-day streak, which breaks the “No streaks” rule
findings.description: §1 says “No game over... No streaks, no shame,” but the chapter win is “You beat it when it runs a full week with you doing only the human parts” — a streak by definition. The document doesn't say what a missed day does to a chapter in progress: if the week resets, that is streak pressure; if it doesn't, the chapter win means nothing. Chapters are the only macro-progression structure, so this choice controls pacing of the whole playthrough. Five chapters means at least five calendar weeks, with no stated rule for what happens after a slip.
findings.passage_referenced: §1 Win/loss, “Win a chapter” and “No game over” bullets; §2 Progression (“Slip, and it gets a bit overgrown”)
findings.omission_noted: No rule for what a missed day does to a chapter in progress
findings.fix_direction: Define chapter completion with tolerance (e.g. “5 of 7 days”) or as a count of successful cycles. State what a slip costs and how long recovery takes.
findings.round2_change_note: Kept MAJOR, strengthened: Player Psychologist F5 independently found the hidden streak; QA F3 adds that a “!” raised at 23:59 can break a chapter from outside the player's control.

findings.title: Progression is front-loaded and runs on two separate tracks that never connect
findings.description: Street cred (habits kept → “new buildings appear,” “No number”) and Loadout (“Every skill or connector you load is a program, and a building”) both produce new buildings and nothing defines how they relate. The Construct shows “every skill and MCP connector out there” in the first hour and the player loads mail immediately, which contradicts the chapter order where mail comes online last. The document says “Five minutes in, you've played the whole game,” but nothing unlocks between minute 5 and chapter 5: no new verbs, agent types, autonomy tier, or escalating demand. Street cred has no number, so no thresholds, decay rate, or recovery rate; a designer can't tune it and a player can't read it beyond “a bit overgrown.”
findings.passage_referenced: §2 Progression (no XP; street cred; loadout); §2 The first hour: the Construct (“every skill and MCP connector out there”, “load mail”); §1 Win/loss chapter order (“pets, household, gym, business, mail”)
findings.omission_noted: No link between the two tracks; no street-cred value, thresholds, decay, or recovery; nothing unlocks mid-game
findings.fix_direction: Gate connector loading behind chapters, or make chapters be the loadout unlocks. Give street cred a hidden internal value with defined decay and recovery. State which buildings come from which track.
findings.round2_change_note: One claim corrected, kept MAJOR: “can be maxed in hour one” overstated it — the Construct loads sample connectors and the real swap is a later act. The corrected finding is worse for pacing: the real loadout track is paced by external setup friction, not by play, and still conflicts with the chapter order.

findings.title: The long-term win has no mechanical hook, and the autonomy dial (its only lever) is cut off from feedback
findings.description: The stated long-term goal is “needing the game less and agents doing more.” The only system that moves agents toward doing more is the autonomy dial, and “You set trust; agents never earn it on their own.” Nothing tells the player when raising trust is justified: no per-agent track record, no approval/rejection count, no suggestion from the twin. The endgame system has no inputs, outputs, or measure of progress. Meanwhile “Win the day: every ‘!’ answered” scales with assigned work and how low the dials are: a cautious player at “ask before anything” gets the most “!”s and the hardest days, while a player at full autonomy wins days trivially. The difficulty curve depends on this unmentioned interaction.
findings.passage_referenced: §1 Win/loss (“Win the day”; “The long-term win...”); §2 What you do, Set autonomy (“You set trust; agents never earn it on their own”); §3 ask_player twin rule
findings.omission_noted: No track record, no trust feedback, no observable long-term-win measure
findings.fix_direction: Show each agent's history (blueprints approved/rejected, keycards returned clean). Have the twin propose raising the dial and let the player confirm. Define the long-term win as an observable measure, e.g. “!”s per task going down over weeks.
findings.round2_change_note: Upgraded to BLOCKING: combined with QA F4 and Narrative F1, both win conditions reward the strategy that disables the safety model, and the long-term goal has no measurable quantity. Rewards point opposite to the guardrails and thesis; not fixable by tuning alone.

findings.title: The worm stock runs down with no refill loop
findings.description: Flora's worm stock is the one fully specified resource (:consumes [:stock 1] every 2 days, warning at :<= :stock 2), but restocking is never defined. Purchases “always need you,” so restocking must be a player chore, yet no restock chore, purchase event, or receipt-to-stock rule appears. The showcase resource only counts down; the warning sign comes up and nothing turns it back into an action. Minor because it is a data gap, not structural, but it is the reference example that “the same code path runs a horse,” so the gap carries to every declared creature.
findings.passage_referenced: §2 Your life as data (the Clojure Flora block); §3 Guardrails (“Purchases... always need you”; “learns your life only from what you connect (receipts...)”)
findings.omission_noted: No restock chore, purchase event, or receipt-to-stock rule
findings.fix_direction: Add a :restock chore triggered by the stock threshold, with purchase confirmation through the player, and a receipt-ingest path that increments :stock.
findings.round2_change_note: Upgraded to MAJOR (not BLOCKING): QA's double-count and spoofing points show the only fully specified resource is unreliable in the MVP's signature moment (week 3, the snap), but fixes are cheap and local.

findings.title: The central thesis (“the world sends you back to your life”) is stated but structurally reversed
findings.description: The game says it exists to send you back to your life (“the game exists to prevent it”; “the long-term win is needing the game less”), but every structure the document defines pulls the game further into the player's life. Chapters bring more of life online each week. You play “everywhere your agent lives,” so replying “fed” to a text counts as playing and being jacked out still means being in the game. “Win the day” requires every “!” answered — clearing in-game obligations, not time away. Street cred and loadout reward more connection. The Architect passage celebrates the opposite of the thesis (“expands out into real life”). Morpheus's “I can only show you the door” is used to welcome the player into the estate rather than out of the illusion. The anti-OASIS promise appears in Section 1 and nowhere in loops, progression, or win conditions.
findings.passage_referenced: §1 thesis / Ready Player One framing; “Win a chapter”; Platform (“everywhere your agent lives”); “Win the day”; Progression; Architect passage; Construct line “I can only show you the door”
findings.omission_noted: No narrative endpoint or recurring beat for “needing the game less”
findings.fix_direction: Add a narrative endpoint or recurring beat: a chapter ending with a world that runs itself, a reachable closing state, or the twin encouraging the player to stay away longer.
findings.round2_change_note: Stays BLOCKING, evidence corrected: the forced jack-out and bedtime lock are partial mechanical carriers of the thesis and should have been credited. But they are stretch, not MVP; bypassable; under pressure to become overridable; and limit session length, not dependency. Nothing in progression or endgame pays off “needing the game less.”

findings.title: The “fixed” cast contradiction isn't fixed: who is the protagonist, and who is the Oracle for anyone who isn't Michael?
findings.description: The document claims the cast is resolved (“the player is Neo, your agent is your twin, the Oracle is the author”) but still contradicts itself. Both the player (“You are Neo... the whole world turns on you”) and the twin (“The Hero or Heroine (Hal) ★ one wow”) get the hero role. The twin is your body, plays Morpheus in the Construct, and is the Hero — three roles with no explanation. “You're its hands in the physical one” puts the human in service of the agent. The Oracle is “the author (Michael), who designed the path and approves every change,” which is meaningless for any other player; “eventually you become your own Oracle” is vague; and “The Director (Michael, human; the Oracle) approves every change” mixes the dev crew with the in-game cast. “Hal” is the author's twin, not the player's, under “batteries not included.”
findings.passage_referenced: Closing line of the document (cast resolution); §1 “You are Neo”; §4 “The Hero or Heroine (Hal)”; §1 twin description; Construct (twin plays Morpheus); Oracle definition; §4 Director line; “Your agent: Hal”
findings.omission_noted: No cast list for a player who is not the author
findings.fix_direction: One cast list for a non-author player with one role per character: protagonist, mentor, and what the Oracle is in a stranger's copy.
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR, strengthened by Business Analyst F3 and Feasibility Lead F5 (the cast was written from the author's chair).

findings.title: Real stakes plus a “no shame” cozy tone, with no defined in-world response to real failure or real loss
findings.description: The document puts real harm on the line (“The only real loss is in real life: Flora goes hungry, you miss your kid's game”) while promising “No streaks, no shame” and an agent that “never shames or compares.” It never says what the world says or shows when a real creature goes unfed — the hardest emotional moment has no tone or script. A real animal going hungry is treated the same as overgrown grass (“a little overgrown, never ruined”). “You miss your kid's game” is invisible to the game. Memorial pets bring grief into the design, but there is no transition for when a real twinned creature dies; under the twin rule a dead pet's twin would keep saying “I'm hungry” until someone edits the data.
findings.passage_referenced: Win/loss (“The only real loss is in real life...”; “No streaks, no shame”); Pillar 1 “Real, not simulated”; missed-day consequence; memorial pets; twin rule (“Flora is a real axolotl”)
findings.omission_noted: No in-world voice for a missed real chore; no live-to-memorial flow for a real creature that dies
findings.fix_direction: Define the in-world voice and staging for a missed real chore under the no-shame rule, and a player-initiated flow for a real creature becoming a memorial.
findings.round2_change_note: Upgraded to BLOCKING: QA F5 reached the dead-pet case independently, and QA F1 shows Flora's worm count is self-reported with no restock. Flora's worm count and the snap are week 3, inside the MVP, so the emotional centerpiece ships without truth guarantee, tone for failure, or path for death — a certainty for any player with a real pet.

findings.title: The emotional peaks are written in film quotes the document says won't ship, and the borrowed metaphor is inverted without comment
findings.description: The document says “the shipped game uses original names and dialogue,” but Signature Moment #2 is named “I know kung fu” and the first hour is built from “Welcome to the Construct,” “I know kung fu” / “Show me,” the weapons rack, and “I can only show you the door.” Remove those lines and the onboarding has no dialogue, with no replacement proposed. Separately, the metaphor is inverted: in the film machines use humans and the real world is the escape; here machines are benevolent and the human is “its hands in the physical one.” The epigraph asks “What is even real anymore?” and the twin rule answers it flatly (“a ‘!’ always means a real question”). Strong irony or an accident — the document doesn't say.
findings.passage_referenced: Film-reference disclaimer (“the shipped game uses original names and dialogue”); §2 Signature Moment #2; §2 The first hour: the Construct; epigraph; twin rule
findings.omission_noted: No original lines for the Construct or “load a program” moment; no statement on whether the inverted Matrix relationship is intended
findings.fix_direction: Write original lines for the Construct and the load-a-program moment, and add a sentence on whether the inversion is intended.
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR: IP half strengthened by Business Analyst F5 (redesign, not renaming); inverted-metaphor half strengthened by QA F2. Not BLOCKING because the fix is writing work, not structural rework.

findings.title: The supporting cast are job titles, not characters; the Architect gets a room and no scene
findings.description: The cozy management/life-sim genre depends on characters with wants, voice, and relationships, but apart from the twin the cast has only functions. Workers are “each a persistent crew persona” with no trait, want, or sample line; the Clerk, Keeper, and Pepper are described only by what they do. The Writer “writes your agent's voice,” but under “batteries not included” the player's own agent is the twin — whose voice is it? The Architect gets the most vivid setup (“a wall of monitors... that wall is all he sees,” Wizard of Oz framing) and never appears in the core loop, day, Construct, or signature moments. Flora's only dialogue is “I'm hungry.”
findings.passage_referenced: Worker personas; Clerk, Keeper, Pepper rows; Writer role; Architect passage; Flora's dialogue
findings.omission_noted: No motivation or sample line per recurring character; no scene for the Architect
findings.fix_direction: One line of motivation and one sample line per recurring character; either a scene for the Architect or remove him from the cast.
findings.round2_change_note: Partially withdrawn, stays MINOR: withdraws the bullet asking for more voice for Flora (a real axolotl with one honest status line is correct under the twin rule, per QA F5). Softens the Architect bullet — his room is in no week of the schedule, so cut him for v1. The Writer-vs-player's-agent voice question stands.

findings.title: The first hour runs on the sample version, and the switch to “real” has no design
findings.description: The only onboarding is the Construct, and it uses pretend parts throughout: a practice job, a pretend chore, a scripted worker. The selling pillar (“it's literally true”) doesn't appear until the player connects their own agent, logins, mail, calendar, and machines, and the document never describes that moment: when, what prompts it, how long it takes, or what the player sees if OAuth or the local Babashka bridge fails. Effects: choice overload at the worst moment (a rack of “every skill and MCP connector out there” shown to someone with no context, “load one” with no recommendation), and a cliff right after the tutorial high where the next step is leaving the game to do account plumbing — the classic quit point.
findings.passage_referenced: §2 The first hour: the Construct (“A rack of every skill and MCP connector out there...”; “The phone rings with a pretend chore”); §1 Batteries not included (“every connection comes with a sample version... swap in the real parts one at a time”); Pillar 1; Audience
findings.omission_noted: No designed first-real-connection moment, target time, failure state, or payoff
findings.fix_direction: Script a first-real-connection moment: one recommended connector (probably the player's own agent), a target completion time, a failure state handled in the fiction, and an estate payoff clearly bigger than the sample version.
findings.round2_change_note: Stays BLOCKING, recommendation narrowed: given Feasibility F3, the first real connection should be the player's own agent or local data, never an OAuth-gated service. Adopts Systems F3 chapter-gating; drop “every connector out there” from the Construct.

findings.title: Waiting is the main thing the player does, and the document doesn't fill it
findings.description: The core loop's payoff (“see the result in the world”) comes after the longest wait in the game: a small task at ~2.5M input tokens takes minutes. The design handles latency visually (“characters animate thinking”) but not how the player spends the time. “You can walk away” assumes there is something to walk to; besides tending creatures (on real fixed schedules) there is nothing to do between “!”s, and no XP, collecting, or exploring. The player assigns a task and watches a progress glow — a terminal with nicer graphics. The Construct's “make that rock rounder” sets an expectation of quick turnaround that real tasks won't deliver, and players who learn “assign, then wait” will leave, eroding the jack-out/jack-in rhythm.
findings.passage_referenced: §4 Constraints (“real agents take seconds to minutes... you can walk away, replies arrive as events”); Token budget (Assign ~2.5M in); Core loop; Progression “no XP”
findings.omission_noted: No activity designed for wait time
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR, worse in the MVP: with the “!” walk-up outside the MVP (Feasibility F1, BA F1), the MVP player can't walk away and be summoned back — they can only watch.

findings.title: Approval fatigue, and “spatial over textual” doesn't work for most of what gets approved
findings.description: Every blueprint example is visual (a river, a rock, terrain), but most real work is not: code changes, mail triage, a Stripe item needing a signature. A ghosted rock can be judged at a glance; a ghosted refactor can't. The player either rubber-stamps (undercutting the safety story that “blueprints, keycards, and the QA gate catch a bad path”) or drops into a diff and reads text (breaking Pillar 2). Since “every change” needs approval and trust never grows on its own, approvals rise with every task — the textbook setup for habituated clicking and resentment. The document doesn't say what a non-visual blueprint looks like, how approvals batch, or whether the game ever suggests raising an agent's autonomy.
findings.passage_referenced: Mechanics table “Approve: Changes appear first as a blueprint, a ghosted version”; “Set autonomy... You set trust; agents never earn it on their own”; §4 “The Director... approves every change”; Pillar 2 “Spatial over textual”; §1 “a workshop for each code repo”
findings.omission_noted: No non-visual blueprint design, no approval batching, no stance on suggesting autonomy raises
findings.round2_change_note: Upgraded to BLOCKING: combined with QA F2 (forgeable “!”), approval fatigue is the mechanism that makes the safety model fail in practice. A design handling real mail, messages, and Stripe can't depend on attention its own loop wears down.

findings.title: Forced jack-outs and the bedtime lock have no override, so the game feels paternalistic to the exact audience it targets
findings.description: The audience is “people who already run an AI agent,” and the estate holds their repos, mail, and business — in practice a work tool. The document freezes the world and locks it with no snooze, no “finish this approval first,” no emergency key, and no handling for an urgent “!” at 10:58 pm. Removing autonomy reliably breeds resentment, and adults lose patience with software that decides when they're done. A hard lock will read as blocking access to their own work, not care; players will turn bedtime off or leave. The document also doesn't say what happens to a pending “!” when the door locks.
findings.passage_referenced: Pillar 4 (“jacks you out when life needs you and locks the door at bedtime”); A day is one round step 3 (“The phone booth rings and the world freezes gently”) and step 5 (“The door locks until morning”); §1 “or cuts you off (bedtime)”
findings.omission_noted: No override, snooze, or emergency key; no rule for a pending “!” at lock time
findings.fix_direction: A negotiable version: snooze with a cost the fiction acknowledges, “finish current blueprint,” or a clear one-tap override; define the fate of a pending “!” at lock time.
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR, reframed: QA F3 shows the lock can't be enforced anyway, so the pillar promises a lock it can't deliver. Fix is to frame closing time as a nudge the player authored, not to add enforcement.

findings.title: The win conditions are driven by agent behavior the player doesn't control, and “no shame” contradicts the overgrowth mechanic
findings.description: Three faults. (1) “Win the day” depends on agents: the “!” count depends on assigned work and ask_player frequency, so a heavy user can't clear the queue before bedtime and loses the day for being engaged. (2) A chapter is a hidden streak: “runs a full week with you doing only the human parts” is a seven-day streak; if a miss resets it, “No streaks” is false, if not, the win is undefined; the first chapter win arrives a week in with no intermediate feedback. (3) Overgrowth is a shame signal: a returning lapsed player is shown how long they were gone, a well-documented reason players don't come back. Underneath, “needing the game less” means short-term rewards must carry all motivation, and right now they are clearing an uncontrolled queue and avoiding overgrowth.
findings.passage_referenced: Win/loss (“Win the day: every ‘!’ answered, your own chores done, and you jacked out by bedtime”; “Win a chapter...”; “No streaks, no shame”; “A missed day leaves the estate a little overgrown”); Street cred (“Slip, and it gets a bit overgrown”); “The long-term win is needing the game less”
findings.omission_noted: No re-entry design for lapsed players; no intermediate chapter feedback
findings.fix_direction: Re-entry design for lapsed players (e.g. the twin having tidied up, or a welcome-back moment) rather than evidence of neglect.
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR, strengthened: chapter-as-streak found independently by Systems F2; “!”-count dependency by Systems F4 and QA F3. Overgrowth sub-point should be read with connection X6 (overgrowth after loss).

findings.title: The MVP cut line leaves out the core loop, and most headline features have no week at all
findings.description: “MVP = weeks 1–4; everything after is stretch,” but “‘!’ walks to you, jack in/out, closing time” is Week 5. The MVP stops before the “!” mechanic — step 2 of the core loop, the subject of the twin rule, and the main expression of Pillar 2 — and Pillar 4 is stretch too, so the committed version doesn't demonstrate the game described. Many core systems are in no week at all: blueprint approve/reject, keycards, the per-agent autonomy dial, night-shift orders and frontier-desk allocation, the Construct, the Architect's room, Clerk/mailbox triage, Pepper/Stripe, and :personality as behavior. There is no cut list, so a reader can't tell what is getting built.
findings.passage_referenced: §4 Scope (7 weeks): “MVP = weeks 1–4; everything after is stretch”; Week 5 line; Core loop definition
findings.omission_noted: No cut list; many core systems unscheduled
findings.fix_direction: An explicit MVP that closes the core loop (talk → assign → work → “!” → answer → approve → world changes) against one mock worker, plus a written list of what is deferred.
findings.round2_change_note: BLOCKING, strengthened: BA F1 and QA F3 reached it independently; adds X1 (the “One wow” is post-MVP by the document's own definition); folds in the former F3 point about Week 2 load (sample connections for every connection in one week).

findings.title: The bridge carries the whole design, and it's unspecified and given one week
findings.description: Pillars 1 and 2 both depend on one Babashka websocket bridge that must normalize live session state from at least three agent runtimes (Hermes, Claude Code, local models), routed through Herdr across two machines, without a model (Observe is $0). The document never says what each runtime exposes to yield “reading / writing / tests passing / stuck / idle”; the event schema the bridge emits; how ask_player is injected into each runtime and how a blocked session resumes when the player answers; or what a “ghosted blueprint” is for a code change (a live second build or branch — a major subsystem). One week, shared with the snap animation, is not enough for a component everything later depends on; if it slips, every later week slips, and no fallback is planned.
findings.passage_referenced: Week 3 (“the bridge: real statuses, Flora's real worm count, the snap end to end”); Token budget Observe ($0, “the bridge reads files and APIs, never a model”); progress glow; Architect/Hermes/Zed/Herdr; ask_player
findings.omission_noted: No per-runtime inputs, event schema, ask_player round trip, code-blueprint definition, or fallback
findings.fix_direction: A one-page bridge spec (inputs per runtime, event schema, ask_player round trip) plus a de-risking spike before Week 2's mock workers commit to a state model.
findings.round2_change_note: BLOCKING, strengthened (X3): the bridge is now the component holding most of the board's unresolved fixes.

findings.title: “Every connection comes with a sample version” doubles the integration surface, and the real integrations have external gates the document leaves out
findings.description: Each connection must be built twice: a believable mock and a real adapter. Packing every mock plus estate, mock workers, and HUD into Week 2 is not credible. The mock strategy is a good testing decision (“the test drive is also the test rig” is the strongest technical idea in the document) but not free. Real integrations have external lead times: Gmail content scopes require Google app verification and a third-party security assessment for distribution beyond test users (weeks to months, costs money); US A2P SMS requires 10DLC registration; an iMessage watcher needs Full Disk Access and an undocumented schema that breaks with OS updates. None blocks a self-hosted demo, but it blocks the stated audience and Pepper's “ready to sell the game.” The document doesn't separate “works for Michael” from “ships to others.”
findings.passage_referenced: “every connection comes with a sample version (pretend inbox, phone, ledger, scripted agents)”; “you play everywhere your agent lives...”; Week 2 (“estate v0, sample connections, three mock workers, HUD”); Constraints table (Gmail OAuth, SMS carrier registration, iMessage local watcher)
findings.omission_noted: No platform-approval lead times; no split between author-only and distributed use
findings.fix_direction: Pick 1-2 connections for the MVP (Flora/chores via local data plus one mock worker), and add platform-approval lead times to the schedule or state that public distribution of real connectors is out of scope.
findings.round2_change_note: Downgraded to MINOR for the 7-week plan: the MVP is explicitly “gradable without a single real account,” so the external gates fall after the course. Remains MAJOR or worse for any real-connector release. The pre-distribution security gate (C2) now matters more.

findings.title: The physics claims don't fit the stated stack
findings.description: (1) three.js's bundled Rapier helper is a thin wrapper for basic rigid bodies; active ragdolls with a balance controller need articulated joints, motor control, and a tuned controller — research-grade work teams spend months on, given one stretch week shared with Flora's swim. (2) “A GPU box for... physics” doesn't hold up: Rapier runs in WASM on the CPU in the browser, and remote physics streamed to a browser frame loop adds network latency to every step. (3) If agents “walk toward you” via ragdoll physics, every “!” depends on pathfinding plus balance stability. The Stack section presents ragdolls as fact while the schedule treats them as stretch.
findings.passage_referenced: Stack (“Physics: Rapier through three.js's own helper. Characters are active ragdolls with a balance controller...; Flora swims as a physical spine”); Architect's “GPU box for local models and physics”; Week 7
findings.omission_noted: No commitment to kinematic locomotion; no explanation of the GPU physics split
findings.fix_direction: Move active ragdolls and the spine swim explicitly to post-v1, state locomotion is kinematic/animated, and remove or explain “GPU box for physics.”
findings.round2_change_note: Downgraded to MINOR: Week 7 is explicitly stretch and no colleague's findings depend on ragdolls. Remaining ask is a one-line kinematic-locomotion commitment and correcting “GPU box for physics.”

findings.title: The production model depends on the product, and on one human's approval bandwidth and plan usage caps
findings.description: Bootstrapping loop: the dev crew is meant to work inside the game's workshop, but the workshop, bridge, and “!” are what the crew is building, so until Week 5 it can't use its own interface; the document doesn't say it works through terminals/Herdr until then. Single approver: with five concurrent agents and “approves every change,” Michael's review time is the throughput ceiling, with no approvals-per-day estimate. Shared, unmeasured quota: the ~2.5M-token Assign cost is an estimate, and building with a five-agent crew and playtesting draw on the same capped plans, so cap exhaustion could stall development for hours per window; neither schedule nor risk table accounts for this.
findings.passage_referenced: Dev crew (“visible as a worker in the game's own workshop”); “The Director (Michael, human; the Oracle) approves every change”; “v1 staffs five”; Token table (Assign ~2.5M in; “the rest are estimates”); “the binding limit is usage caps”
findings.omission_noted: No pre-Week-5 dev workflow, approvals-per-day estimate, or production token budget
findings.fix_direction: State the pre-Week-5 dev workflow outside the game, measure Assign cost on a real task, budget production token usage separately from play, and set an approval-batching policy for the Director.
findings.round2_change_note: MAJOR, unchanged, strengthened by X4 (Director is the first approval-fatigue test subject) and X6 (token economics hit the build schedule first).

findings.title: Marking a chore done is unverified, sent from several channels, and can't be undone, so the worm count stops being “literally true”
findings.description: Pillar 1 promises Flora's “2 worms left” is literally true, but the count is calculated from player reports (:consumes [:stock 1] per :feed). Three channels (“Reply ‘fed’ to a text, click the canal, or tell your agent. Every channel sends the same event”) with no duplicate handling. Double counting: text “fed,” then click the canal to see the snap — two worms gone. Cheating “Win the day”: clicking the canal without feeding completes the chore; “Flora goes hungry” is exactly what the game can't detect. No restock: :stock only goes down and the warning stays up forever; receipts are named as a data source but nothing maps them to :stock. Spoofing: the SMS channel accepts input, and the doc never says which numbers it accepts texts from.
findings.passage_referenced: §1 Pillar 1; §2 “Mark a chore done”; §2 “The snap”; Flora data block; §4 Scope week 3 (“Flora's real worm count, the snap end to end”) inside the MVP
findings.omission_noted: No duplicate-event rule, no restock event, no sender authentication
findings.fix_direction: Before week 3 can finish: a rule for duplicate events, a restock event, and a rule for who may send the event.
findings.round2_change_note: Stays BLOCKING with a narrower core: per Systems F5, the restock bullet alone is MINOR; the blocking parts are duplicate events and unauthenticated senders. Strengthened by X1 (no provenance at the bridge) and C3 (receipt ingestion as attack path). Synthesis marks this finding WEAKENED on severity (Systems and Feasibility rate it a cheap local fix) and lists it as Quick Win 1.

findings.title: “A ‘!’ always means a real question” can be hijacked: the most trusted signal in the UI can be forged through any input that reaches an agent
findings.description: The doc treats “!” as trustworthy because it only appears via ask_player, but any agent that has read attacker-controlled content can call ask_player — “real question” means an agent really asked, not that the question is legitimate. Open paths: the Clerk “holds no keys” but writes the triage summary, and nothing says whether it is passed to Hal, who holds the loadout and hands out keycards. The Construct loads “every skill and MCP connector out there” in seconds; unvetted MCP servers are the “poisoned tools” the Red Team should cover, but the Red Team “attacks only pretend services,” so real connectors are never tested. The guardrail “Purchases and messages to other people always need you” assumes the player is a reliable gate; a forged “!” with a plausible approval request uses that gate against them, and Pillar 2 trains the player to act before reading.
findings.passage_referenced: §3 twin rule (ask_player guarantee); §3 Clerk row and Guardrails; §2 The first hour: the Construct; §4 Red Team row; §4 “The test drive is also the test rig”
findings.omission_noted: No provenance or trust boundary for ask_player; real connectors never red-teamed
findings.round2_change_note: Stays BLOCKING, strengthened: Feasibility F2 confirms ask_player transport is unspecified; X2 shows the doc's own onboarding breaks the guarantee; C1 shows two colleagues' proposed fixes would expand the attack surface.

findings.title: Closing time is easy to bypass and leaves a lot of work stuck when it triggers, and the MVP doesn't include it at all
findings.description: Easy to bypass: “Bedtime is declared data,” so set it to 04:00 and the lock never happens; and since you play “everywhere your agent lives” and “You could do all of this at a terminal,” locking the browser only locks the 3D view. Undefined at lock time: keycards still out, unapproved blueprints, and a night worker who hits a question at 3 a.m. (shown in the opening scene) sits idle until morning, wasting the scarce frontier desk. “Win the day” can be blocked from outside: an agent raising “!” at 23:59 makes the day unwinnable. MVP contradiction: jack in/out, closing time, and “!” walking are week 5, so the MVP lacks Pillar 4, step 2 of the core loop, and the Construct's sparring match; the MVP cannot run the first hour.
findings.passage_referenced: §1 Platform line, Pillar 4, “Win the day”; §2 A day is one round steps 4–5; §2 “Hand out a keycard”; §2 Construct; §4 Scope
findings.omission_noted: No enforcement across channels; no rule for work in flight at lock time
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR; one point withdrawn and one handed off. Withdraws “set bedtime to 04:00” as an exploit (player choosing bedtime is agency, per Psych F4); the real issue is that the lock is incoherent across channels (C2). Hands the “MVP contradiction” bullet to Feasibility F1 and BA F1 as high-confidence BLOCKING under their findings.

findings.title: The autonomy dial contradicts “approves every change”
findings.description: “Set autonomy: a dial per agent, from ask before anything to fully autonomous,” but changes appear first as a blueprint (“Approve and it becomes real”), “The Director... approves every change,” and purchases and messages “always need you.” Either full autonomy skips blueprint approval (contradicting §4 and Pillar 1) or it doesn't (the dial controls nothing — a fake control). The doc never says which actions the dial covers. Does a fully autonomous night desk apply its “stack of blueprints at breakfast” overnight while nobody can review? And “Win a chapter” needs a week “with you doing only the human parts” — approving and handing out keycards are human parts, so winning quietly pushes players to raise autonomy, against the guardrails.
findings.passage_referenced: §2 action table (“Approve,” “Set autonomy,” “Hand out a keycard”); §1 “Win a chapter”; §3 Night crew row; §4 “The Director... approves every change”
findings.omission_noted: No definition of which actions each dial setting covers
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR, scope widened: Systems F4 and Psych F5 independently found “Win the day” depends on dial settings; together with “Win a chapter” pushing autonomy up, the win conditions consistently reward weakening the guardrails — a systems problem and a safety problem at once.

findings.title: The highest-priority jack-outs have no data source, and creatures have no way to die or be rehomed
findings.description: Interrupt sources: the jack-out order is household (“Dinner!”) → creatures (“Biscuit at the door with his leash”) → appointments → deadlines, but “household members are never agents... in v1” and SMS “covers opted-in people only; the bot texts only the player,” so nothing produces “Dinner!”. “Biscuit at the door” sounds like a sensor reading but the data model only supports scheduled chores, not presence — a timer pretending to be real, breaking Pillar 1 and the twin rule. Collisions: nothing covers two simultaneous interrupts or what “the world freezes gently” means for a “!” agent walking to you. Real pet death: no :status, no move from active to :memorial; the Keeper keeps showing “I'm hungry” over a dead axolotl and missed feedings keep the estate overgrown, breaking “never shames” at the worst time.
findings.passage_referenced: §2 A day is one round step 3; §2 Your life as data (Flora block, virtual/memorial pets, “household members are never agents”); §3 twin rule and Guardrails; §4 SMS constraint row
findings.omission_noted: No data source for household/presence interrupts; no collision rule; no death/rehome state
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR: pet-death part strengthened by Narrative F3 (X5); interrupt-collision part gains the delivery-failure case from Feasibility F4 (X4).

findings.title: A quota-stalled agent has no visible state and its keycard is never returned
findings.description: The twin rule says “!” appears only when an agent calls ask_player. An agent whose plan hits its usage cap mid-task can't call any tool, ask_player included, so it never raises “!” and keeps its progress glow; Pillar 2's promise to show “who's busy, blocked, or waiting on you” fails silently. Its keycard “comes back when the task ends,” which never happens, so keycards stay out indefinitely (a credential leak) and a scarce frontier desk stays occupied.
findings.passage_referenced: §3 twin rule (“only” via ask_player); §4 usage caps (“the binding limit is usage caps, not dollars”); Pillar 2; §2 “Hand out a keycard”
findings.omission_noted: No bridge-set “stalled” state; no keycard timeout
findings.fix_direction: The bridge needs a “stalled” state that it sets on its own, separate from ask_player, plus a keycard timeout.
findings.round2_change_note: New finding in Round 2. No single Round 1 review found it; it follows from combining the twin rule with the usage-cap constraint raised by Systems F1, Feasibility F5, and BA F4.

findings.title: The 4-week MVP does not contain the core loop, the win condition, or the main pillar
findings.description: The core loop depends on “!”, but “‘!’ walks to you” is week 5 (stretch). Jack in/out and closing time are week 5 — that is Pillar 4, the Executive Summary's key differentiator (“the OASIS keeps you in… This world nudges you out”), and two of three “Win the day” conditions. Street cred and the first life chapter are week 6 — all progression and “Win a chapter.” Not scheduled at all: the Construct, “I know kung fu” (the “One wow”), keycards, the autonomy dial, and blueprint approve/reject as a deliverable. So the MVP is an estate with mock workers, a working snap, and chat bubbles — no reason-to-play signal, no win state, no jack-out: the terminal-with-a-skin the document sets out to beat.
findings.passage_referenced: §4 “Scope (7 weeks)” read against §1 Core loop, Win/loss, Design pillars, and §2 Signature moments and The first hour
findings.omission_noted: Core loop signal, win state, jack-out, progression, and signature moment absent from the MVP
findings.fix_direction: Re-cut the MVP around the loop. Move “!” and jack-out/closing time ahead of streaming chat polish. Name one signature moment as must-ship. Cut or explicitly defer the Construct.
findings.round2_change_note: Stays BLOCKING, narrower ask (C2): a static “!” marker plus closing time in the MVP; walking “!” and ragdolls deferred.

findings.title: The document is several products at once
findings.description: At least five products share one pitch, each with its own audience and success metric: (1) an agent-orchestration front end for developers; (2) a life-management/habit app; (3) a pet/creature sim including memorial pets; (4) a household coordination platform (“Someday it goes multiplayer”); (5) a self-building dev pipeline shown as a game (the 15-role dev crew). Only #1 and the creature half of #3 (the snap) are load-bearing; #2 is half load-bearing. Memorial pets, multiplayer twins, and the 15-role crew are decoration at this stage, each with its own integration, privacy, and content load. The document never says which it is when they conflict — e.g. agents running a business task at bedtime: productivity tool (keep working) or wellness product (lock the door)?
findings.passage_referenced: §1 “Win a chapter”; §2 “Your life as data” (memorial pets, :personality, multiplayer); §3 cast table (Pepper, Clerk); §4 “Agent roles: the dev crew”
findings.omission_noted: No ranking of which product is primary
findings.fix_direction: One sentence: “Prime Meridian is primarily X; Y is a supporting system; Z is out of scope for v1.”
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR, strengthened by X1 and X5; C1 shows it is the decision underneath the Pillar 4 dispute.

findings.title: The audience is undefined and contradicts itself
findings.description: At least three incompatible audiences: “people who already run an AI agent” (narrow, technical); “a game for all and none,” “everyone's game,” “anyone can play with no accounts” (broad, casual); and the author himself (“both Oracle and Neo”; cast named after his bot and pet; reference setup of Hermes in Zed driving Herdr across a Mac and GPU box with a Babashka bridge and iMessage watcher). The kit-car framing puts the integration burden on the player, fitting only the technical audience and arguably only users of this exact toolchain. The casual audience would only see sample/demo mode — a fake version of “Real, not simulated.” Nothing describes a non-author player: what they own, what they set up, and how long before the first snap.
findings.passage_referenced: §1 epigraph, “The cast” (Oracle), Genre/Platform/Audience line, “Batteries not included”; §2 “everyone's game”; §4 Stack
findings.omission_noted: No non-author player persona, minimum accounts/hardware, or time-to-first-snap
findings.fix_direction: Name one primary player persona who is not Michael, list minimum required accounts and hardware, and check that the first hour works for them.
findings.round2_change_note: Upgraded to BLOCKING: X3 (every approver is Michael) shows the missing persona is the root cause behind Psych F1, Feasibility F3, and Narrative F2; none can be fixed until the non-Michael player is defined.

findings.title: There is no business model, yet the document plans to sell and puts real running costs on the player
findings.description: The dev crew includes a Business Manager keeping “the company ready to sell the game,” but nothing says what is sold, to whom, or for how much. “One play session… is about $7 at API prices” — roughly $200/month for daily play on top of any price. The answer (“runs on flat-rate plans, so the binding limit is usage caps”) makes playability depend on the player's third-party subscriptions and vendor terms the studio doesn't control. The kit-car model means the product is mostly the player's own accounts, and the GDD links a public GitHub, so it's unclear what a customer pays for. Comparable products are free/subscription agent dashboards and premium cozy games with zero running costs; Prime Meridian has the cost profile of the first and the pitch of the second.
findings.passage_referenced: §4 Token budget ($7 session; flat-rate note); dev crew row “Business Manager (Pepper)”; §1 “Batteries not included”
findings.omission_noted: No pricing, distribution, or competitor section
findings.fix_direction: Add a short section: what is sold (chassis? hosted bridge? content packs?), who pays model costs, and the nearest comparables.
findings.round2_change_note: Stays MAJOR with a correction: the ~$200/month figure extrapolates from estimates (only Talk turns were measured), so it is illustrative. Finding stands because it is about the missing model. Per X4, becomes BLOCKING the moment Pepper's sales work starts.

findings.title: The hook and the first hour are built on licensed-film IP the document says it will remove
findings.description: The disclaimer says “the shipped game uses original names and dialogue,” but the design vocabulary is Matrix vocabulary: “You are Neo,” the Oracle, the Architect, Morpheus, “jack in,” “I know kung fu” (a named signature moment), “Welcome to the Construct,” the weapons rack, “I can only show you the door.” The first hour is a scene-by-scene reenactment with no original replacements; once references come out, the onboarding, the second signature moment, and much of the tone must be redesigned, not renamed — unscoped work. The main differentiator leans on the OASIS/Ready Player One comparison, positioning against a film rather than products the audience uses (agent dashboards, habit trackers).
findings.passage_referenced: §1 “The cast” and film-reference disclaimer; §2 Signature Moment #2; §2 The first hour: the Construct
findings.omission_noted: No original-IP replacements; no positioning against real competitors
findings.fix_direction: Draft original-IP versions of the cast roles and the Construct now, before they are built, and position the game against real competing products.
findings.round2_change_note: Upgraded to MAJOR: Round 1 rated it “MINOR (upgrade to MAJOR if the shipped game is commercial)”; the condition is already met (Pepper keeps the company “ready to sell the game”). Narrative F4 adds that the replacement isn't find-and-replace.

cross_exam_engagement.round2_summary: Agrees the thesis is reversed but insists the fix is economic, not narrative; proposes closing time as a scoring condition; disputes QA F1 as BLOCKING; defends overgrowth as the only negative feedback. Finds that both win conditions make maxing autonomy the dominant strategy. Upgrades F4 to BLOCKING and F5 to MAJOR.

Accepts an override on the bedtime lock only if staged visibly; rejects auto-tidying where real creatures were neglected; disputes BA's MINOR rating of film IP; warns a falling “!” rate measures agent dependence. Finds the MVP contains zero expression of the thesis. Upgrades F3 to BLOCKING; partially withdraws F5.

Argues the bedtime bypass is healthy and closing time should be an honest nudge; keeps only the double-count part of QA F1 as BLOCKING; asks for capped decay and fast recovery. Connects approval fatigue with the forged “!” as a safety gate set up to fail. Upgrades F3 to BLOCKING.

Rates QA F1 as MAJOR with cheap fixes; scopes QA F2 to a real-connector release gate; proposes a buildable MVP order; rejects a live cap gauge; puts the Construct script off the critical path. Shows the bridge has absorbed most of the board's open problems. Downgrades F3 and F4 to MINOR.

Objects that twin-proposed autonomy raises would be the prime forged-“!” target; says the bedtime lock is both too strong and too weak and the product must choose; keeps F1 BLOCKING for duplicates and unauthenticated senders. Adds a new MAJOR finding: quota-stalled agents look busy forever.

Argues an overridable lock erases the only differentiator and escalates it as a product decision; insists closing time belongs in the MVP; says the thesis must be written into the business model. Finds every approver in the design is Michael. Upgrades F3 to BLOCKING and F5 to MAJOR.

cross_exam_conflicts.summary: The thesis reversal is in the economy, not the story: each chapter adds domains, agents, and ask_player calls, so the “!” count driving “Win the day” rises every week. A dialogue beat can't offset that. The fix must be a measured quantity designed to fall (“!”s per task, minutes jacked in) plus chapters that move work off the player before adding domains.

cross_exam_conflicts.nature: proposes a third position on closing time
cross_exam_conflicts.summary: Psych says the lock is too hard, QA says too soft; both treat closing time as enforcement, which the document can't support. Make it a scoring condition only (“jacked out by bedtime” is already a win-the-day clause): the override comes free (you just don't win the day) and the bypass stops being an exploit. A no-cost snooze would quietly delete a win clause; any override must be visible in the win state.

QA found real problems (dedupe across channels, SMS spoofing), but not BLOCKING: a dedupe window per due period, a :restock rule, and a sender allowlist are a few lines each — a quick win. QA's point that the game can't detect Flora went hungry is a separate Pillar 1 truth-claim issue no schema fixes.

Overgrowth is the only negative feedback in the economy; removing or auto-tidying it makes street cred a one-way ratchet with no information. Cap overgrowth and make recovery fast (one kept habit clears a visible chunk) instead — which requires the internal number asked for in F3.

The bedtime lock and forced jack-out are the only mechanics carrying the thesis; a freely skippable lock leaves the anti-OASIS promise as rhetoric. Let the player override, but never invisibly: the world and twin must stage it (lights dimming, the twin staying up, the porch light on). The player must feel the door even if they walk through it.

A twin that quietly tidies while a real axolotl went unfed makes the world lie, the exact “fake passed off as real” the twin rule forbids. Separate two kinds of neglect: estate neglect is cosmetic and can be tidied without shame; neglect of a real creature or person must be told truthfully in the twin's kind voice.

BA rates film IP by legal/commercial exposure (MINOR unless commercial); Narrative rates it by whether the emotional beats exist without the quotes, and they don't. Unscoped redesign of a signature moment is MAJOR regardless of sale. BA's point that the differentiator is positioned against a film also sharpens Narrative F1.

A falling “!” rate measures “agents doing more,” not “needing the game less.” A player who hands everything to fully autonomous agents scores perfectly while becoming more dependent. The observable long-term win needs a human-side counterpart (time jacked out, chores done in person), or the endgame makes the inversion official.

The bedtime bypass is the healthiest part of the design. A lock covering only the 3D view can't be enforced, so presenting it as a lock teaches players the rules are theater; adding enforcement would worsen resentment for a work-tool audience. Rewrite Pillar 4 as a nudge the player authored (“you asked me to send you home”) with an explicit, cheap escape hatch. Agrees with QA that lock-time hanging state is undefined.

cross_exam_conflicts.nature: disputes framing, keeps part of finding
cross_exam_conflicts.summary: Marking Flora fed without feeding her is self-deception on an honor-system tracker; designing against the player pushes toward surveillance, against “never shames.” The BLOCKING part is the double count: an honest player who texts “fed” then clicks the canal sees the jar go wrong — the world visibly lying. Fix duplicates first; treat self-report fraud as out of scope.

Decay on absence turns a return visit into a guilt screen. If street cred decays, cap it fast (a day or two looks like a month) and front-load recovery. Systems' cap-window gauge has the same tension: show scarcity at the moment of allocation, not as a permanent draining HUD meter of the player's real quota.

BA lists memorial pets as decoration. Psychologically they are one of the few features creating attachment to the place rather than the to-do list. Cut them or design them; half-done is worst because the live-to-memorial transition is where a dead pet keeps saying “I'm hungry.” Keep them only with a player-initiated transition flow.

MAJOR from a build standpoint. The :feed :every “2d” due window is a natural idempotency key (one completion per window), restock can be a manual player event, and sender allowlisting is one config line on an SMS adapter the MVP doesn't need. What can't be engineered is verification, so Pillar 1 should be reworded to “literally what you reported.”

The MVP is mock-only (“without a single real account”), so the forged “!” has no entry point inside the committed build; it blocks connecting real accounts, not the 7-week plan. QA is right that the test rig gives false comfort afterwards. Gate: no real connector ships until ask_player events carry provenance and Clerk output never feeds an agent holding keycards.

“!” can't come before talk: the answer goes through the Week 4 conversation channel and needs the ask_player round trip. Buildable order: bridge spike, then talk plus a static “!” marker in the MVP, walking deferred. Jack in/out and closing time are cheap UI states and can move into the MVP as BA asks — supported.

No data source exists for a live cap gauge; on vendor-enforced flat-rate plans the reliable signal is reactive (limit hit). A guessed gauge would violate the twin rule. Alternative: frontier desk count as declared data (fixed N) and a “desk went dark: cap reached” event.

The Construct is in no week of the schedule; writing original dialogue for an unscheduled feature spends effort before onboarding is buildable. Supports BA's “cut or explicitly defer the Construct”; scope the script once it is scheduled.

A twin-proposed dial raise arrives as a “!” via ask_player, making “give me more autonomy” the normal request and the most valuable one for an injected agent to forge. Track records can be gamed with trivial clean tasks. “Agents never earn it on their own” is the only line blocking escalation. Show the track record, but no agent (twin included) may start a trust change; any proposal must come from game code over a channel ask_player can't reach and look visibly different.

cross_exam_conflicts.nature: both true; forces a product decision
cross_exam_conflicts.summary: Psych says the lock is too strong, QA says it is too weak; both are true. The design annoys the compliant player (loses the 3D view at 23:00) and does nothing to the compulsive one (switches to the terminal). The doc must decide: enforcement (every channel respects it) or nudge (override fine, reword Pillar 4). BA F2 raises the same fork; three lenses reach the same unmade decision.

Agrees missing restock alone is a data gap. F1 stays BLOCKING for duplicate events and unauthenticated senders. Systems' receipt-ingest fix makes things worse: receipts arrive by mail, read by the Clerk, whose output can be poisoned, so a crafted receipt could set Flora's real worm count. Restock must be authenticated like the “fed” path.

Pillar 4 is the only differentiator from free agent dashboards. A bypassable lock (QA F3) plus a one-tap override makes it a cosmetic setting. Not a UX question: if the product is a dev tool, take the override and drop Pillar 4 as headline; if it is the “sends you back to your life” game, in-fiction negotiation is fine but a free bypass is not. The board should escalate this.

cross_exam_conflicts.nature: agrees on severity, disputes MVP content
cross_exam_conflicts.summary: Feasibility's MVP closes the agent loop but leaves Pillar 4 out, proving an orchestration UI rather than the pitched game. Narrowed ask given Feasibility F2/F4: a static “!” marker (no locomotion) and closing time (clock, world-state change, locked-door scene — doesn't touch the bridge). Cutting the cheapest pillar to protect the most expensive is backwards.

A success metric of declining use clashes with any engagement-priced model (subscription, hosted bridge, content packs). Without settling monetization, someone will quietly cut a “world that runs itself” ending. The thesis must be written into the business model too (one-time purchase, player-paid tokens, no engagement KPIs).

cross_exam_connections.title: Max autonomy is the dominant strategy, and it runs against the guardrails
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: “Win the day” is easiest at full autonomy (fewer “!”s) and “Win a chapter” rewards doing only the human parts, so both win conditions are optimized by maxing every dial, with no counter-pressure. A player following the rewards removes the human checkpoint §3 and §4 rely on.

cross_exam_connections.title: “Win the day” has no output
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Street cred is fed by habits kept, not by winning the day, and nothing says what a won day produces. Psych and QA argue the day win is unfair; it is also inert — the short-term reward Psych says must carry all motivation doesn't exist as a system.

cross_exam_connections.title: The MVP has no progression and no strategic decision
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The committed v1 contains no real decision, no chapter, no street cred or loadout, and no “!” to drive difficulty. Pacing and the difficulty curve can't be playtested until week 6, the second-to-last week.

cross_exam_connections.title: Loadout progression is the onboarding cliff
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Swapping in a real part is the “I know kung fu” moment, so the loadout track is the undesigned sample-to-real migration. Its pacing is set by OAuth, carrier registration, and Full Disk Access, not by any designed curve.

cross_exam_connections.title: Waiting time has no meta layer to absorb it
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: About three world-changing payoffs per session, each behind a minutes-long wait. Management games fill idle time with spending, upgrading, or planning; here progression has no number or thresholds. The dead-time problem and “nothing unlocks between minute 5 and chapter 5” are the same hole.

cross_exam_connections.title: The MVP doesn't ship the thesis
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Jack in/out and closing time are week 5 stretch, so the 4-week MVP contains zero expression of the game's reason to exist — the OASIS with a pet. Any re-cut should treat at least one jack-out beat as thematically mandatory.

cross_exam_connections.title: The red-pill moment is unwritten
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The switch from sample to real has no design, and the Matrix framing has a ready-made beat for it — the red pill — which the document skips. “I can only show you the door” hands off to account plumbing; the moment the world becomes “literally true” has no scene, line, or payoff.

cross_exam_connections.title: The theme the document closed is reopened by the exploit
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The twin rule answers “What is even real anymore?” flatly, but a “!” can be forged — so the film's real theme (don't trust the interface) applies, while Pillar 2 trains the opposite. Either embrace it (the twin teaches the player to question a “!”) or stop invoking the film's epistemology.

cross_exam_connections.title: The moral hierarchy and the sensor hierarchy are inverted
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: What the narrative says matters most (household, kids, a creature's welfare) is exactly what the system can't see; what it sees perfectly (repo status, agent state) the fiction ranks lowest. The game's emotional priorities exist only in prose.

cross_exam_connections.title: The cast was written from the author's chair
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: For the author, the production model and the fiction are the same thing, so “the Oracle approves every change” is true on his machine and meaningless elsewhere. Two other lenses independently confirm the cast gap.

cross_exam_connections.title: The Construct spoils the arc
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The chapter order is the story arc, but the Construct hands out mail (the last chapter) in hour one and “I know kung fu” delivers the whole loadout at once. The arc has no rising action, so any thesis endpoint has nothing to build toward.

cross_exam_connections.title: Approval fatigue + forged “!” = the safety gate is set up to fail
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Approvals multiply, most are non-visual, and Pillar 2 trains acting on “!” without reading. By week two a habituated player approves a crafted malicious request with the same click as fifty harmless ones. The purchases/messages guardrail relies on attention the reward structure drains.

cross_exam_connections.title: The reward structure pushes players to stop reviewing
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Every motivational pressure tells the player to raise autonomy and approve faster; nothing makes caution rewarding. Endorses Systems' track-record fix and adds that careful review needs a visible payoff, e.g. a rejected blueprint that caught something real is celebrated in-world.

cross_exam_connections.title: The first-real-connection cliff is steeper: the obvious first connector may be impossible for non-author players
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Gmail content scopes require Google verification; iMessage needs Full Disk Access against an undocumented schema; casual players only ever see sample mode. The first real connection must be the player's own agent or local chore data, never mail. Mail being last chapter yet handed out first is also an onboarding bug.

cross_exam_connections.title: The onboarding is unscheduled and has lost its script
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The most retention-critical stretch has no build slot, no final script, and no hand-off to real play. The MVP lacks “!” and jack-out, so week-4 playtests can't produce first-hour data; the team will reach launch without watching a non-author player go through onboarding.

cross_exam_connections.title: Waiting meets usage caps
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: At ~2.5M tokens per task on capped plans, a long wait can end with a cap hit instead of a result — the worst payoff, for reasons never shown. Hitting a cap must be a designed in-world event (desks go dark until a stated time), not a silent stall.

cross_exam_connections.title: Overgrowth after loss
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: A grieving player who stays away returns to an overgrown estate and a hungry axolotl that no longer exists — the single worst emotional moment in the design, following entirely from existing rules. BLOCKING for any release beyond the author.

cross_exam_connections.title: The Director is the first casualty of approval fatigue
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Michael approves every change from a five-agent crew and is also the reference player. If he burns out, habits like batch-approving get baked into the design unexamined. Measure approvals per day during production as a preview of the player experience.

cross_exam_connections.title: Signature Moment #2 can't happen in the MVP, by the document's own definitions
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: “Swapping in a real part is the ‘I know kung fu’ moment,” and the MVP works “without a single real account.” The “One wow” runs only post-MVP on real connectors — the surface QA shows unsafe and Feasibility shows externally gated. The headline moment sits behind every unresolved risk.

cross_exam_connections.title: Restock via receipts runs through the riskiest pipe in the system
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Receipts arrive as mail: Gmail restricted scopes, read by the Clerk (which reads untrusted mail), whose output would modify game state. A spoofed receipt could reset a real animal's food counter. In v1, restock is a manual player event; receipt ingest waits for provenance.

cross_exam_connections.title: The bridge picks up a new requirement from nearly every colleague
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The unspecified bridge is now expected to provide idempotency keys, ask_player provenance, presence events with no sensor source, non-visual code blueprints, cap state, and per-runtime enforcement of every autonomy-dial setting (requiring permission models the document never describes). One week of schedule carrying most of the board's open problems.

cross_exam_connections.title: The Director is the first approval-fatigue test subject
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Player-side rubber-stamp fatigue and the Director approving every change from five agents are the same problem at two levels; production shows it first. Log approvals per day and time per approval in Weeks 2–5 to inform batching/autonomy design. The Director line is about production, though the in-game blueprint vs. full-autonomy contradiction still stands.

cross_exam_connections.title: The bedtime lock can only be soft
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The only enforceable lock is on the browser view; agents stay reachable in Zed and by text. The override comes free, and a hard lock can't be built without revoking the player's own agent access. Describe Pillar 4 as a nudge with a fiction-acknowledged override — cheaper than either alternative.

cross_exam_connections.title: The token economics hit the build schedule before they hit the customer
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The same estimated (unmeasured) 2.5M-token Assign cost limits development: five crew members on the same capped plans as playtesting. If the estimate is off by 2x, play pacing and the 7-week build slip together.

cross_exam_connections.title: The bridge has no stated authentication, so both “!” and “fed” can be forged locally as well as via prompt injection
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: No event has defined provenance. If ask_player is an MCP tool, any connector loaded from the Construct rack runs in the same harness and could register the same tool name or post to the socket; any local process could mark Flora fed. The bridge spec must say who may send each event type, or the twin rule can't be enforced at the transport layer.

cross_exam_connections.title: The Construct breaks the twin rule on purpose, and the sample-to-real switch makes “!” ambiguous
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The Construct's scripted worker raises the player's first “!”, which isn't a real question. During the mixed sample/real period there's no visual difference, so players either dismiss a real “!” or get fooled by a sample-shaped prompt. Sample entities must be visibly marked until the switch to real.

cross_exam_connections.title: An agent that runs out of quota can't ask for help, so it looks busy forever
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: A capped agent can't call ask_player, keeps its progress glow, and never returns its keycard (credential leak, desk occupied). Needs a bridge-set “stalled” state and a keycard timeout. Became new finding adversarial-qa:F6 (MAJOR).

cross_exam_connections.title: A “!” that has to walk to you can fail to arrive
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Under ragdoll locomotion a worker can fall, stick, or fail to path; the doc doesn't say whether an undelivered “!” still counts as pending for “Win the day.” Kinematic locomotion fixes it; otherwise delivery needs a fallback such as a HUD indicator after N seconds.

cross_exam_connections.title: Pet death: agreement plus a mechanical consequence
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: A dead Flora's :feed chore still counts toward “your own chores done,” so the player can't win the day without faking a feeding or editing data while grieving. Asks the moderator to treat it as one strengthened finding.

cross_exam_connections.title: Two progression tracks exist because they belong to two different products
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Loadout is the dev-tool product's progression; chapters and street cred are the life-management product's. They don't interlock because they were designed for different players. Gating connectors behind chapters only works after a primary product is chosen.

cross_exam_connections.title: “Every skill and MCP connector out there” is the most dangerous feature creep in the document
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Three reviewers flagged the rack for choice overload, forgeable “!” via unvetted tools, and a maxed-out progression track; none framed it as scope. It is an open-ended commitment to support and secure an uncontrolled ecosystem, in an unscheduled feature. One curated connector fixes all three — the best cost-to-impact cut in the document.

cross_exam_connections.title: Every approver in the design is Michael
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: The design assumes player, developer, approver, and reference hardware owner are the same person — the document has only been written for one user. Root cause behind several findings on the board.

cross_exam_connections.title: Selling the game carries recurring compliance costs and liability no business model covers
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Google verification and 10DLC are recurring costs; the safety guarantee behind mail, messages, and Stripe can be forged. Who is liable when a forged “!” gets a player to approve a payment? Making players register their own OAuth clients narrows the audience further. Pepper's sales plan can't proceed until integrations and liability ownership are settled.

cross_exam_connections.title: Real pet death is a decorative feature turning into a support burden
cross_exam_connections.combined_insight: Memorial pets implicitly promise a live-to-memorial flow nobody specified; a twin saying “I'm hungry” over a dead animal becomes a support ticket and review-score problem. Recommendation changes to: defer memorial pets, but spec the minimal death/rehome state for live creatures in v1.
